i18n.en: And the two messengers came to Sodom at evening; and Lot sat at the gate of Sodom; and Lot saw them, and rose up to meet them; and he bowed himself with his face to the earth,

paragraphs.commentary: *Shnei ha-malakhim* — *the two messengers*. The arithmetic of Gen 18's *three men* (*shloshah anashim*, v 2) here resolves: at Gen 18:22 *the men* turned toward Sodom while Avraham stood before YHWH; the two who continued to Sodom arrive here at evening. The Mamre / Sodom diptych (Letellier 1995) pairs the day-half at the oaks with the night-half at the city gate. The translation preserves *messengers* per the *malakh-yhwh-messenger* convention (Gen 16 onward), declining the conventional *angels* which imports later angelology. The *appliesTo* of both the *malakh-yhwh-messenger* and *shloshah-anashim-three-visitors-theophany* entries are extended in glossary v2.16.0 to include this verse.

i18n.en: and they called unto Lot, and said unto him: Where are the men that came in to you this night? Bring them out unto us, that we may know them.

paragraphs.commentary:
*Hotzi'em eleinu v-neda otam* — *bring them out unto us, that we may know them*. The chapter's hinge-verse and the reception-history flashpoint of the entire Sodom narrative. The verb *yada* (to know) carries a documented sexual sense in the HB (Gen 4:1, *v-ha-adam yada et-Chavvah* — *and the man knew Eve*; Judg 19:22-25, the verbatim parallel-scene at Gibeah), and the demand is read by the great majority of modern scholars as a sexual demand. The chapter's reception then bifurcates sharply.

The Christian patristic and medieval tradition (Augustine, Aquinas; the medieval penitentials) read the demand as the textual ground of the *sodomy* category — the place-name *Sodom* becoming, through Latin *sodomia*, the English *sodomy*. The reading was the standard Western Christian reception from late antiquity through the early modern period and remains the popular-cultural association of the chapter today.

The modern critical reading (Sarna *JPS Genesis* 1989 pp. 134-136; Brueggemann *Genesis* Interpretation 1982; Letellier *Day in Mamre, Night in Sodom* 1995 chs 4-5; Tornkvist *Eros Defiled?* 1998; Carden *Sodomy: A History of a Christian Biblical Myth* 2004 — full-length monograph; Loader *A Tale of Two Cities: Sodom and Gomorrah* 1990) reads the scene as a *gang-rape-violence directed at outsiders* / *hospitality-violation* episode, distinct from any claim about orientation. The HB's own characterization of Sodom's sin elsewhere is decisive evidence for this reading: Ezek 16:48-50 enumerates Sodom's iniquity as *pride, fullness of bread, prosperous ease, and failure to strengthen the hand of the poor and needy* — not as same-sex contact. The Gen 18:20-21 *outcry* (see *zaaqah-outcry-of-the-oppressed*) is the cry of victims, paralleled at Gen 4:10 (Abel's blood) and Exod 2:23-25 (Israel in Egypt); the structure presupposes ongoing oppression-of-the-vulnerable, not a single sexual episode. The Judg 19 Gibeah parallel — where a Levite's concubine is in fact handed over and gang-raped to death — makes the violence-and-outsider-abuse reading editorially explicit in the wider canon.

The translation preserves the literal *that we may know them*, preempting neither reading. The full bifurcation is documented in the *sodom-as-sodomy-reception-vs-inhospitality* glossary entry.

paragraphs.text: וַיֹּאמַ֑ר אַל־נָ֥א אַחַ֖י תָּרֵֽעוּ׃

i18n.en: And he said: I pray you, my brothers, do not so wickedly.

paragraphs.text: הִנֵּה־נָ֨א לִ֜י שְׁתֵּ֣י בָנ֗וֹת אֲשֶׁ֤ר לֹֽא־יָדְעוּ֙ אִ֔ישׁ אוֹצִֽיאָה־נָּ֤א אֶתְהֶן֙ אֲלֵיכֶ֔ם וַעֲשׂ֣וּ לָהֶ֔ן כַּטּ֖וֹב בְּעֵינֵיכֶ֑ם רַ֠ק לָֽאֲנָשִׁ֤ים הָאֵל֙ אַל־תַּעֲשׂ֣וּ דָבָ֔ר כִּֽי־עַל־כֵּ֥ן בָּ֖אוּ בְּצֵ֥ל קֹרָתִֽי׃

i18n.en: Behold now, I have two daughters who have not known a man; let me, I pray you, bring them out unto you, and do you to them as is good in your eyes; only unto these men do nothing, since they have come under the shadow of my roof.

paragraphs.commentary:
*Hineh-na li shtei vanot ... v-asu lahen ka-tov b-eyneykhem* — *Behold, I have two daughters ... do to them as is good in your eyes*. Lot offers his two virgin daughters to the mob in place of the messengers. The narrator records the offer without editorial comment; the mob does not accept it (vv 9-11) and the daughters are not in fact handed over, but the offer is made.

The verse has acquired heavy modern feminist-critical reception. Trible (*Texts of Terror*, 1984) reads the parallel offer at Judg 19:22-25 — where the Levite's concubine *is* in fact handed over and gang-raped to death by the men of Gibeah — as the structurally explicit working-out of the Lot-offer logic: when the daughter-or-concubine-trade is in fact accepted, the consequence is the woman's death. Fewell and Gunn (*Gender, Power, and Promise*, 1993) read the offer as evidence of the patriarchal narrative's acceptable *trade* of female bodies for male hospitality-honor, with the narrator's silence participating in the structure it records. Bach (*Women, Seduction, and Betrayal in Biblical Narrative*, 1997/1999) and Exum (*Plotted, Shot, Painted*, 1996) extend the reading across the wider corpus.

The ancient hospitality-and-honor reading (Westermann *Genesis 12-36* 1985 pp. 301-303; Sarna *JPS Genesis* 1989 p. 136) reads the offer as an extreme expression of the ANE host-protects-his-guests obligation: the host's honor is so bound to the protection of those *under the shadow of his roof* that he will offer his own daughters in their place. Both readings can be held in apparatus: the offer's *ANE-hospitality logic* is real; the *modern ethical critique* of that logic is also serious work. The translation preserves the ASV-baseline *do to them as is good in your eyes* literally; the apparatus carries the bifurcation.

paragraphs.text: וַיֹּאמְר֣וּ ׀ גֶּשׁ־הָ֗לְאָה וַיֹּֽאמְרוּ֙ הָאֶחָ֤ד בָּֽא־לָגוּר֙ וַיִּשְׁפֹּ֣ט שָׁפ֔וֹט עַתָּ֕ה נָרַ֥ע לְךָ֖ מֵהֶ֑ם וַיִּפְצְר֨וּ בָאִ֤ישׁ בְּלוֹט֙ מְאֹ֔ד וַֽיִּגְּשׁ֖וּ לִשְׁבֹּ֥ר הַדָּֽלֶת׃

i18n.en: And they said: Stand back. And they said: This one fellow came in to sojourn, and he will play the judge; now will we deal worse with you than with them. And they pressed sorely upon the man, even Lot, and drew near to break the door.

paragraphs.text: וַיִּשְׁלְח֤וּ הָֽאֲנָשִׁים֙ אֶת־יָדָ֔ם וַיָּבִ֧יאוּ אֶת־ל֛וֹט אֲלֵיהֶ֖ם הַבָּ֑יְתָה וְאֶת־הַדֶּ֖לֶת סָגָֽרוּ׃

i18n.en: But the men put forth their hand, and brought Lot into the house to them, and shut the door.

paragraphs.text: וְֽאֶת־הָאֲנָשִׁ֞ים אֲשֶׁר־פֶּ֣תַח הַבַּ֗יִת הִכּוּ֙ בַּסַּנְוֵרִ֔ים מִקָּטֹ֖ן וְעַד־גָּד֑וֹל וַיִּלְא֖וּ לִמְצֹ֥א הַפָּֽתַח׃

i18n.en: And they struck the men that were at the entrance of the house with blindness, both small and great; so that they wearied themselves to find the entrance.

paragraphs.commentary: *Va-yaku ba-sanverim* — *they struck them with blindness*. The lexeme *sanverim* (סַנְוֵרִים) is one of only two HB occurrences of the term — here at Gen 19:11 and at 2 Kgs 6:18 (Elisha's prayer striking the Aramean army at Dotan). The two attestations are structurally parallel: a divine-or-prophetic blinding of a hostile group surrounding a protected house or city. The plural form is itself unusual — the ordinary HB term for blindness is *ivvaron* (singular). HALOT and Tigay (*JPS Excursus*) note the possible Akkadian loanword from *šunwurum* (dazzling, blinding-by-light), suggesting a flash-of-light sense rather than ordinary loss of sight; the alternative West-Semitic and Aramaic derivations are documented but less clearly motivated. The translation preserves the ASV-baseline *blindness*; the *dazzling-light* nuance is carried in the *sanverim-blindness-hapax* glossary entry.

paragraphs.text: וַיֹּאמְר֨וּ הָאֲנָשִׁ֜ים אֶל־ל֗וֹט עֹ֚ד מִֽי־לְךָ֣ פֹ֔ה חָתָן֙ וּבָנֶ֣יךָ וּבְנֹתֶ֔יךָ וְכֹ֥ל אֲשֶׁר־לְךָ֖ בָּעִ֑יר הוֹצֵ֖א מִן־הַמָּקֽוֹם׃

i18n.en: And the men said unto Lot: Have you here any besides? Son-in-law, and your sons, and your daughters, and whomever you have in the city, bring them out of the place;

paragraphs.text: כִּֽי־מַשְׁחִתִ֣ים אֲנַ֔חְנוּ אֶת־הַמָּק֖וֹם הַזֶּ֑ה כִּֽי־גָֽדְלָ֤ה צַעֲקָתָם֙ אֶת־פְּנֵ֣י יְהוָ֔ה וַיְשַׁלְּחֵ֥נוּ יְהוָ֖ה לְשַׁחֲתָֽהּ׃

i18n.en: for we will destroy this place, because the outcry of them has grown great before YHWH; and YHWH has sent us to destroy it.

paragraphs.commentary: *Ki gadlah tza'aqatam et-pnei YHWH* — *for their outcry has grown great before YHWH*. The verse cycles the *za'aqah / tza'aqah* lexeme of Gen 18:20-21 back to its conclusion: the *outcry against Sodom* that triggered the divine investigation at Mamre now becomes the explicit rationale for the destruction. The *zaaqah-outcry-of-the-oppressed* entry (already governing this verse) documents the cross-corpus distribution at Gen 4:10 (Abel), Exod 2:23-25 (Israel in Egypt), Exod 22:22-24 (the widow-and-orphan formula), Job 34:28 and the Psalter; the consensus reading is *outcry of the oppressed*, not of the perpetrators — corroborated by Ezek 16:48-50's enumeration of Sodom's sin as oppression of the poor.

paragraphs.text: וַיֵּצֵ֨א ל֜וֹט וַיְדַבֵּ֣ר ׀ אֶל־חֲתָנָ֣יו ׀ לֹקְחֵ֣י בְנֹתָ֗יו וַיֹּ֙אמֶר֙ ק֤וּמוּ צְּאוּ֙ מִן־הַמָּק֣וֹם הַזֶּ֔ה כִּֽי־מַשְׁחִ֥ית יְהוָ֖ה אֶת־הָעִ֑יר וַיְהִ֥י כִמְצַחֵ֖ק בְּעֵינֵ֥י חֲתָנָֽיו׃

i18n.en: And Lot went out, and spoke unto his sons-in-law, who were to marry his daughters, and said: Arise, get out of this place; for YHWH will destroy the city. But he seemed unto his sons-in-law as one that jested.

paragraphs.commentary: *Va-yhi ki-m'tzacheq b-eynei chatanav* — *and he was as one who jested in the eyes of his sons-in-law*. The verb is the piel participle *m'tzacheq* of the same root (*tzachaq*) as Avraham's and Sarah's disbelief-laughter at Gen 17:17 and 18:12-15 and the name *Yitzchaq* of Gen 17:19 (see *yitzchaq-name-etymology-laughter-pattern*). The Genesis editor's placement is editorially deliberate: the same root that names the covenant-son's laughter immediately re-occurs, in the piel-mocking sense, at the moment Lot's sons-in-law disregard the warning of destruction. The *appliesTo* of the laughter-pattern entry is extended in glossary v2.16.0 to include this verse, marking it as the piel-mockery instance in the wider patriarchal *tzachaq* cluster (qal disbelief and joy at 17:17 / 18:12-15 / 21:6; piel mockery and play at 19:14 / 21:9 / 26:8 / Exod 32:6).

paragraphs.text: וּכְמוֹ֙ הַשַּׁ֣חַר עָלָ֔ה וַיָּאִ֥יצוּ הַמַּלְאָכִ֖ים בְּל֣וֹט לֵאמֹ֑ר קוּם֩ קַ֨ח אֶֽת־אִשְׁתְּךָ֜ וְאֶת־שְׁתֵּ֤י בְנֹתֶ֙יךָ֙ הַנִּמְצָאֹ֔ת פֶּן־תִּסָּפֶ֖ה בַּעֲוֺ֥ן הָעִֽיר׃

i18n.en: And when the dawn arose, then the messengers hastened Lot, saying: Arise, take your wife, and your two daughters that are here, lest you be consumed in the iniquity of the city.

paragraphs.text: וַֽיִּתְמַהְמָ֓הּ ׀ וַיַּחֲזִ֨קוּ הָאֲנָשִׁ֜ים בְּיָד֣וֹ וּבְיַד־אִשְׁתּ֗וֹ וּבְיַד֙ שְׁתֵּ֣י בְנֹתָ֔יו בְּחֶמְלַ֥ת יְהוָ֖ה עָלָ֑יו וַיֹּצִאֻ֥הוּ וַיַּנִּחֻ֖הוּ מִח֥וּץ לָעִֽיר׃

i18n.en: But he lingered; and the men laid hold upon his hand, and upon the hand of his wife, and upon the hand of his two daughters, YHWH being merciful unto him; and they brought him forth, and set him without the city.

paragraphs.commentary: *B-chemlat YHWH alav* — *in YHWH's pity upon him*. The lexeme *chemlah* (חֶמְלָה — pity, sparing, compassion-to-spare-from-destruction) is a marked HB term distinct from the more common *chesed* (covenant loving-kindness) and *rachamim* (womb-compassion). The *chemlah* sense is specifically *sparing-from-deserved-or-imminent-destruction*: cf. 1 Sam 15:3-15 (Saul's *chemlah* on Agag, explicitly contrasted with the *cherem* command); 2 Sam 12:4 (the *chemlah* in Nathan's parable, the rich man's failure to spare from his own flock); Mal 3:17 (YHWH's *chemlah* on those who fear him *as a man spares his son who serves him*); Joel 2:18; Jon 4:10-11 (YHWH's *chemlah* on Nineveh); Ezek 9:5 (the negative formula — *al-tachos eynkhem v-al-tachmolu* — *let not your eye spare, do not have pity*). The Gen 19:16 occurrence is the lexeme's first HB attestation and the only patriarchal-narrative instance, structurally pairing with the v 29 *va-yizkor Elohim et-Avraham* — the divine-remembrance and divine-sparing together constitute the mechanism of Lot's deliverance.

paragraphs.text: וַיְהִי֩ כְהוֹצִיאָ֨ם אֹתָ֜ם הַח֗וּצָה וַיֹּ֙אמֶר֙ הִמָּלֵ֣ט עַל־נַפְשֶׁ֔ךָ אַל־תַּבִּ֣יט אַחֲרֶ֔יךָ וְאַֽל־תַּעֲמֹ֖ד בְּכָל־הַכִּכָּ֑ר הָהָ֥רָה הִמָּלֵ֖ט פֶּן־תִּסָּפֶֽה׃

i18n.en: And it came to pass, when they had brought them forth abroad, that he said: Escape for your life; do not look behind you, nor stay in all the Plain; escape to the mountain, lest you be consumed.

paragraphs.commentary:
*Al-tabit acharekha* — *do not look behind you*. The do-not-look-back prohibition. The Hebrew uses the verb *navat* (hiphil — to look intently, gaze) rather than the more general *ra'ah* (to see); the v 26 fulfillment uses the same root (*va-tabet ishto me-acharav*). The formula has heavy downstream reception. The NT recall at Luke 17:32 — *mnemoneuete tes gynaikos Lot* — *remember Lot's wife* — uses Lot's wife's looking-back as a typological warning in Jesus's apocalyptic discourse on the day of the Son of Man.

The do-not-look-back / do-not-touch / do-not-eat prohibition is also a widespread ANE and cross-cultural narrative pattern (the Orpheus-and-Eurydice myth in Greek; the Sumerian *Descent of Inanna*; the Akkadian Adapa myth's do-not-eat warning). The pattern is documented in comparative mythology as the *taboo-on-the-threshold* type-scene. The cross-cultural parallel is noted here as comparative-mythological observation, not as direct evidence of literary dependence; the WoH lens does not extend further into project-distinctive synthesis from this verse.

paragraphs.text: וַיֹּ֥אמֶר ל֖וֹט אֲלֵהֶ֑ם אַל־נָ֖א אֲדֹנָֽי׃

i18n.en: And Lot said unto them: Oh, not so, my lord.

paragraphs.text: הִנֵּה־נָ֠א מָצָ֨א עַבְדְּךָ֣ חֵן֮ בְּעֵינֶיךָ֒ וַתַּגְדֵּ֣ל חַסְדְּךָ֗ אֲשֶׁ֤ר עָשִׂ֙יתָ֙ עִמָּדִ֔י לְהַחֲי֖וֹת אֶת־נַפְשִׁ֑י וְאָנֹכִ֗י לֹ֤א אוּכַל֙ לְהִמָּלֵ֣ט הָהָ֔רָה פֶּן־תִּדְבָּקַ֥נִי הָרָעָ֖ה וָמַֽתִּי׃

i18n.en: Behold now, your servant has found favor in your sight, and you have magnified your loving-kindness, which you have shown unto me in saving my life; and I cannot escape to the mountain, lest evil overtake me, and I die.

paragraphs.text: הִנֵּה־נָ֠א הָעִ֨יר הַזֹּ֧את קְרֹבָ֛ה לָנ֥וּס שָׁ֖מָּה וְהִ֣יא מִצְעָ֑ר אִמָּלְטָ֨ה נָּ֜א שָׁ֗מָּה הֲלֹ֥א מִצְעָ֛ר הִ֖וא וּתְחִ֥י נַפְשִֽׁי׃

i18n.en: Behold now, this city is near to flee unto, and it is a little one. Oh let me escape there — is it not a little one? — and my life shall live.

paragraphs.text: וַיֹּ֣אמֶר אֵלָ֔יו הִנֵּה֙ נָשָׂ֣אתִי פָנֶ֔יךָ גַּ֖ם לַדָּבָ֣ר הַזֶּ֑ה לְבִלְתִּ֛י הָפְכִּ֥י אֶת־הָעִ֖יר אֲשֶׁ֥ר דִּבַּֽרְתָּ׃

i18n.en: And he said unto him: See, I have accepted you concerning this thing also, that I will not overthrow the city of which you have spoken.

paragraphs.text: מַהֵר֙ הִמָּלֵ֣ט שָׁ֔מָּה כִּ֣י לֹ֤א אוּכַל֙ לַעֲשׂ֣וֹת דָּבָ֔ר עַד־בֹּאֲךָ֖ שָׁ֑מָּה עַל־כֵּ֛ן קָרָ֥א שֵׁם־הָעִ֖יר צֽוֹעַר׃

i18n.en: Hasten, escape there; for I cannot do anything until you come there. Therefore the name of the city was called Tzo'ar.

paragraphs.commentary: *Al-ken qara shem-ha-ir Tzo'ar* — *therefore the name of the city was called Tzo'ar*. The folk-etymology of *Tzo'ar* (צוֹעַר) from the *tza'ar / mitzar* (small / little one) root deployed at v 20 (*ha-ir ha-zot ... v-hi mitzar* — *this city ... and it is a little one*). The translation transliterates *Tzo'ar* per the WoH patriarchal-place-name convention; the etymological pun is preserved at the lexical level via the *little one* rendering at v 20. The town is identified by tradition with the southeastern Dead Sea zone (Deut 34:3 *kikkar Yericho ... ad-Tzoar*; Isa 15:5; Jer 48:34, in the Moab oracles). No separate glossary entry; the etymology is documented in commentary only.

paragraphs.text: הַשֶּׁ֖מֶשׁ יָצָ֣א עַל־הָאָ֑רֶץ וְל֖וֹט בָּ֥א צֹֽעֲרָה׃

i18n.en: The sun was risen upon the land when Lot came unto Tzo'ar.

paragraphs.text: וַֽיהוָ֗ה הִמְטִ֧יר עַל־סְדֹ֛ם וְעַל־עֲמֹרָ֖ה גָּפְרִ֣ית וָאֵ֑שׁ מֵאֵ֥ת יְהוָ֖ה מִן־הַשָּׁמָֽיִם׃

i18n.en: Then YHWH rained upon Sodom and upon Amorah sulfur and fire from YHWH out of the heavens;

paragraphs.commentary:
*Va-YHWH himtir al-Sodom v-al-Amorah gophrit va-esh me-et YHWH min ha-shamayim* — *Then YHWH rained upon Sodom and upon Amorah sulfur and fire from YHWH out of the heavens*. The chapter's destruction-verse contains two of the most-cited formulae in the entire Hebrew Bible.

*Gophrit va-esh* — *sulfur and fire*. The phrase is the HB's canonical destruction-formula and recurs across the corpus with editorial deliberation. Deut 29:22 (*gophrit va-melach srefah kol-artzah* — *sulfur and salt, a burning, all its land*, in the curse-list); Job 18:15 (*y-zoreh al-navehu gophrit* — *sulfur is scattered on his habitation*); Isa 30:33 (*nishmat YHWH k-nachal gophrit bo'erah-bah* — *the breath of YHWH like a torrent of sulfur kindles it*); Isa 34:9 (Edom-oracle, sulfur as the destruction-element); Ezek 38:22 (Gog-Magog oracle, *fire and sulfur* rained on the invader); Ps 11:6 (*yamter al-rasha'im pachim esh v-gophrit* — *snares, fire and sulfur on the wicked*). The NT recall is explicit: Luke 17:29 (the Lot-typology *ebrexen pyr kai theion ap' ouranou* — *it rained fire and sulfur from heaven*); Rev 14:10, 19:20, 20:10, 21:8 (the eschatological *lake of fire and sulfur*). The cross-corpus reach is among the most distributed in the HB.

*Me-et YHWH min ha-shamayim* — *from YHWH out of the heavens*. The verse uses the divine name *YHWH* twice in a single clause: *va-YHWH himtir ... me-et YHWH min ha-shamayim*. The construction can be read as intensifying repetition (the second YHWH simply restating the first) or as referring to two distinct loci of agency — a reading that became the foundational text of the rabbinic *two-powers in heaven* debate. The classical rabbinic engagement is b. Sanhedrin 38b, where a heretic uses this very verse to argue for two divine powers; Rav Chisda's response is that Moses simply wrote the divine name twice. The same verse is load-bearing for early Christian binitarian / Logos exegesis: Justin Martyr's *Dialogue with Trypho* 56-59 uses Gen 19:24 to argue for the Logos as a second divine figure distinct from but coordinate with the Father.

Modern scholarly treatments of the wider two-powers question — Segal *Two Powers in Heaven* (1977), Boyarin *Border Lines: The Partition of Judaeo-Christianity* (2004), Boyarin *The Jewish Gospels* (2012) — read the verse as one of the principal Hebrew Bible texts that second-temple and rabbinic exegetes worked from when articulating positions on divine multiplicity. The two-powers reading is a recognized minority position in both Jewish and Christian reception history. The translation preserves the doubled divine name literally; the apparatus carries the debate. The WoH translation does not preempt the question and does not synthesize a project-distinctive reading from the verse — the lens stays in the wiki and long-form material, not in the glossary or commentary.

paragraphs.text: וַֽיַּהֲפֹךְ֙ אֶת־הֶעָרִ֣ים הָאֵ֔ל וְאֵ֖ת כָּל־הַכִּכָּ֑ר וְאֵת֙ כָּל־יֹשְׁבֵ֣י הֶעָרִ֔ים וְצֶ֖מַח הָאֲדָמָֽה׃

i18n.en: and he overthrew those cities, and all the Plain, and all the inhabitants of the cities, and that which grew upon the ground.

paragraphs.commentary: *Va-yahafokh et-he-arim ha-el* — *and he overthrew those cities*. The verb *hafakh* (to overturn, overthrow) gives the noun *mahapekhah* (the overthrowing) at v 29, and the verb-noun pair becomes the standard HB designation for the Sodom-Amorah destruction. The cross-corpus chain is editorially deliberate: Deut 29:22, Isa 1:7 and 13:19 (Babylon-overthrow explicitly typed to Sodom), Jer 49:18 (Edom-oracle), Jer 50:40 (Babylon-oracle), Amos 4:11 (*k-mahapekhat Elohim et-Sodom v-et-Amorah* — *as Elohim overthrew Sodom and Amorah*, the covenant-lawsuit formula), Lam 4:6 (Jerusalem's punishment compared to Sodom's). *Like the overthrow of Sodom and Amorah* becomes the HB's fixed destruction-comparison.

paragraphs.text: וַתַּבֵּ֥ט אִשְׁתּ֖וֹ מֵאַחֲרָ֑יו וַתְּהִ֖י נְצִ֥יב מֶֽלַח׃

i18n.en: But his wife looked back from behind him, and she became a pillar of salt.

paragraphs.commentary: *Va-t'hi netziv melach* — *and she became a pillar of salt*. The verb *navat* (look intently) is the same as in the v 17 prohibition. The noun *netziv* is from *natzav* (to stand, the root of the *nitzavim* of Gen 18:2 *shloshah anashim nitzavim alav*); the *netziv* has the sense of *one-set-up, fixed-installation*. The verse is the etiology of the salt-formations on the western shore of the Dead Sea — Mt. Sodom / Jabal Usdum, a 235-meter halite-and-marl ridge with multiple anthropomorphic salt-pillars produced by differential erosion, identified across two millennia of pilgrimage and traveler accounts as Lot's wife. Josephus *Antiquities* I.11.4 already references the pillar as a continuing physical site. The Bronze-Age destruction-archaeology of the southeastern Dead Sea (Bab edh-Dhra, Numeira; Rast and Schaub *BASOR* 1974 and *Bab edh-Dhra: Excavations at the Town Site* 2003) provides the modern archaeological context. The translation preserves the ASV-baseline *pillar of salt*.

paragraphs.text: וַיַּשְׁכֵּ֥ם אַבְרָהָ֖ם בַּבֹּ֑קֶר אֶל־הַ֨מָּק֔וֹם אֲשֶׁר־עָ֥מַד שָׁ֖ם אֶת־פְּנֵ֥י יְהוָֽה׃

i18n.en: And Avraham got up early in the morning to the place where he had stood before YHWH;

paragraphs.text: וַיַּשְׁקֵ֗ף עַל־פְּנֵ֤י סְדֹם֙ וַעֲמֹרָ֔ה וְעַֽל־כָּל־פְּנֵ֖י אֶ֣רֶץ הַכִּכָּ֑ר וַיַּ֗רְא וְהִנֵּ֤ה עָלָה֙ קִיטֹ֣ר הָאָ֔רֶץ כְּקִיטֹ֖ר הַכִּבְשָֽׁן׃

i18n.en: and he looked toward Sodom and Amorah, and toward all the land of the Plain, and beheld, and, lo, the smoke of the land went up as the smoke of a furnace.

paragraphs.commentary:
*Alah qitor ha-aretz k-qitor ha-kivshan* — *the smoke of the land went up as the smoke of a furnace*. The verse is one of the most concretely physical destruction-images in the Hebrew Bible. The lexeme *qitor* (thick condensed smoke or vapor) is rare — only here (twice), at Ps 119:83 (*k-nod b-qitor* — *like a wineskin in smoke*), and Ps 148:8 (*esh u-varad sheleg v-qitor*). The lexeme is distinct from the more common *ashan*.

The comparison-noun *kivshan* (כִּבְשָׁן — furnace, kiln) is the load-bearing element. The lexeme recurs at two structurally significant verses. Exod 9:8 — Moses casts *piach kivshan* (soot of the furnace) into the air at the sixth plague of boils. Exod 19:18 — at the Sinai theophany, *va-ya'al ashano k-eshen ha-kivshan* — *its smoke went up as the smoke of the furnace*, the verbatim echo of Gen 19:28. The cross-corpus chain between the Sodom-overthrow's smoke and the Sinai-theophany's smoke is editorially deliberate; the same furnace-simile frames the two paradigmatic divine-fire events of the Pentateuch.

The *kivshan* is the standard ANE pottery-kiln or metallurgical-smelter — a high-temperature confined-combustion device producing thick black smoke. It is distinct from *kur* (smelting-furnace, the figurative *iron furnace* of Egypt at Deut 4:20 / 1 Kgs 8:51 / Jer 11:4). The recent scientific literature on a possible Late-Bronze-Age cosmic-airburst destruction event at Tall el-Hammam in the southern Jordan Valley (Bunch et al. *Scientific Reports* 11, 2021) is one current scientific hypothesis for the geological context of the Sodom-tradition; the hypothesis is contested in the geoarchaeological literature and is cited here as a scientific reading, not as a project-distinctive synthesis. The translation preserves the ASV-baseline *the smoke of the land went up as the smoke of a furnace*.

paragraphs.text: וַיְהִ֗י בְּשַׁחֵ֤ת אֱלֹהִים֙ אֶת־עָרֵ֣י הַכִּכָּ֔ר וַיִּזְכֹּ֥ר אֱלֹהִ֖ים אֶת־אַבְרָהָ֑ם וַיְשַׁלַּ֤ח אֶת־לוֹט֙ מִתּ֣וֹךְ הַהֲפֵכָ֔ה בַּהֲפֹךְ֙ אֶת־הֶ֣עָרִ֔ים אֲשֶׁר־יָשַׁ֥ב בָּהֵ֖ן לֽוֹט׃

i18n.en: And it came to pass, when Elohim destroyed the cities of the Plain, that Elohim remembered Avraham, and sent Lot out of the midst of the overthrow, when he overthrew the cities in which Lot dwelt.

paragraphs.commentary:
*Va-yizkor Elohim et-Avraham* — *Elohim remembered Avraham*. The intercession-arc that opened at Gen 18:23-33 closes here with the *zakhar* (remember) verb. The cross-corpus distribution of divine-remembrance is editorially patterned: Gen 8:1 (*va-yizkor Elohim et-Noach* — at the flood-cessation), Gen 30:22 (*va-yizkor Elohim et-Rachel* — at Yosef's conception), Exod 2:24 (*va-yizkor Elohim et-brito et-Avraham* — at the Exodus prelude), 1 Sam 1:19 (Hannah's conception). The Gen 19:29 occurrence pairs with the v 16 *b-chemlat YHWH* (*chemlat-yhwh-compassion-formula*) — divine-sparing and divine-remembrance together constituting the mechanism of Lot's deliverance.

The divine-name shift is also editorially marked: the chapter has used *YHWH* throughout (vv 13, 14, 16, 17, 21, 24, 27), but here twice uses *Elohim*. The pattern matches the other *zakhar*-mechanism verses (Gen 8:1, Gen 30:22, Exod 2:24, all *Elohim*) and is a P-document compositional marker. The existing *vayyizkor-elohim* entry (originally governing Gen 8:1 only) is extended in glossary v2.16.0 to include this verse and the wider *zakhar*-with-divine-subject cluster.

paragraphs.text: וַיַּעַל֩ ל֨וֹט מִצּ֜וֹעַר וַיֵּ֣שֶׁב בָּהָ֗ר וּשְׁתֵּ֤י בְנֹתָיו֙ עִמּ֔וֹ כִּ֥י יָרֵ֖א לָשֶׁ֣בֶת בְּצ֑וֹעַר וַיֵּ֙שֶׁב֙ בַּמְּעָרָ֔ה ה֖וּא וּשְׁתֵּ֥י בְנֹתָֽיו׃

i18n.en: And Lot went up out of Tzo'ar, and dwelt in the mountain, and his two daughters with him; for he feared to dwell in Tzo'ar; and he dwelt in the cave, he and his two daughters.

paragraphs.commentary: The chapter's coda (vv 30-38) is the etiology of Moab and Ammon — Israel's two transjordan-neighbor peoples — through Lot's daughters' incest with their drunken father. The narrative is one of the canonical HB polemics-against-neighbor-peoples and is the source-text for the Deut 23:4-5 exclusion of Ammonites and Moabites from the assembly of YHWH; see the *moab-ammon-etiology-incest* entry and the commentary at vv 37-38 for full treatment.

paragraphs.text: וַתֹּ֧אמֶר הַבְּכִירָ֛ה אֶל־הַצְּעִירָ֖ה אָבִ֣ינוּ זָקֵ֑ן וְאִ֨ישׁ אֵ֤ין בָּאָ֙רֶץ֙ לָב֣וֹא עָלֵ֔ינוּ כְּדֶ֖רֶךְ כָּל־הָאָֽרֶץ׃

i18n.en: And the firstborn said unto the younger: Our father is old, and there is not a man in the land to come in unto us after the manner of all the land;

paragraphs.text: לְכָ֨ה נַשְׁקֶ֧ה אֶת־אָבִ֛ינוּ יַ֖יִן וְנִשְׁכְּבָ֣ה עִמּ֑וֹ וּנְחַיֶּ֥ה מֵאָבִ֖ינוּ זָֽרַע׃

i18n.en: come, let us make our father drink wine, and we will lie with him, that we may preserve seed from our father.

paragraphs.text: וַתַּשְׁקֶ֧יןָ אֶת־אֲבִיהֶ֛ן יַ֖יִן בַּלַּ֣יְלָה ה֑וּא וַתָּבֹ֤א הַבְּכִירָה֙ וַתִּשְׁכַּ֣ב אֶת־אָבִ֔יהָ וְלֹֽא־יָדַ֥ע בְּשִׁכְבָ֖הּ וּבְקׄוּמָֽהּ׃

i18n.en: And they made their father drink wine that night; and the firstborn went in, and lay with her father; and he knew not when she lay down, nor when she arose.

paragraphs.commentary: *U-v-qumah* — *and when she arose*. The Masoretic text marks the *vav* of *uvqumah* with a supralinear dot — one of the canonical fifteen *puncta extraordinaria* documented in the existing *puncta-extraordinaria-v9-elav* entry (Gen 18:9 list). The rabbinic reading (b. Bava Metzia 87a; Bereshit Rabbah 51:8) reads the dot as marking that Lot in fact *did* know when she arose (even if not when she lay down); the modern text-critical reading (Tov 2012) treats it as an editorial-flag of textual uncertainty. The translation does not represent the dot; it is noted here for consistency with the chapter-18 entry.

paragraphs.text: וַֽיְהִי֙ מִֽמָּחֳרָ֔ת וַתֹּ֤אמֶר הַבְּכִירָה֙ אֶל־הַצְּעִירָ֔ה הֵן־שָׁכַ֥בְתִּי אֶ֖מֶשׁ אֶת־אָבִ֑י נַשְׁקֶ֨נּוּ יַ֜יִן גַּם־הַלַּ֗יְלָה וּבֹ֙אִי֙ שִׁכְבִ֣י עִמּ֔וֹ וּנְחַיֶּ֥ה מֵאָבִ֖ינוּ זָֽרַע׃

i18n.en: And it came to pass on the next day, that the firstborn said unto the younger: Behold, I lay last night with my father; let us make him drink wine this night also, and go in, and lie with him, that we may preserve seed from our father.

paragraphs.text: וַתַּשְׁקֶ֜יןָ גַּ֣ם בַּלַּ֧יְלָה הַה֛וּא אֶת־אֲבִיהֶ֖ן יָ֑יִן וַתָּ֤קָם הַצְּעִירָה֙ וַתִּשְׁכַּ֣ב עִמּ֔וֹ וְלֹֽא־יָדַ֥ע בְּשִׁכְבָ֖הּ וּבְקֻמָֽהּ׃

i18n.en: And they made their father drink wine that night also; and the younger arose, and lay with him; and he knew not when she lay down, nor when she arose.

paragraphs.text: וַֽתַּהֲרֶ֛יןָ שְׁתֵּ֥י בְנֽוֹת־ל֖וֹט מֵאֲבִיהֶֽן׃

i18n.en: Thus were both the daughters of Lot with child by their father.

paragraphs.text: וַתֵּ֤לֶד הַבְּכִירָה֙ בֵּ֔ן וַתִּקְרָ֥א שְׁמ֖וֹ מוֹאָ֑ב ה֥וּא אֲבִֽי־מוֹאָ֖ב עַד־הַיּֽוֹם׃

i18n.en: And the firstborn bore a son, and called his name Moab; he is the father of the Moabites unto this day.

paragraphs.commentary: *Va-tiqra shemo Moab* — *and she called his name Moab*. The MT does not preserve an explicit etymological gloss for *Moab* (מוֹאָב), but the LXX adds *legousa ek tou patros mou* (*saying: from my father*) — preserving an interpretive etymology *me-av* (*from-father*) that is presupposed by the Hebrew narrative but not stated. The folk-etymology of the place-name from *me-av* (from-father, i.e. by incest) is one of the most editorially marked etymological cases in Genesis.

paragraphs.text: וְהַצְּעִירָ֤ה גַם־הִוא֙ יָ֣לְדָה בֵּ֔ן וַתִּקְרָ֥א שְׁמ֖וֹ בֶּן־עַמִּ֑י ה֛וּא אֲבִ֥י בְנֵֽי־עַמּ֖וֹן עַד־הַיּֽוֹם׃ (ס)

i18n.en: And the younger, she also bore a son, and called his name Ben-Ammi; he is the father of the children of Ammon unto this day.

paragraphs.commentary:
*Va-tiqra shemo Ben-Ammi* — *and she called his name Ben-Ammi*. The folk-etymology of *Ben-Ammi* (literally *son of my people / son of my kin*) is explicit in the verse itself: *ben ammi* — *son of my kin* — i.e. from-within-the-family, the incestuous origin marked at the name-level. The pair-etymology with *Moab* (v 37) frames the transjordan-neighbor-peoples (Moab and Ammon) as descended-from-incest.

The Deut 23:4-5 exclusion of Ammonites and Moabites from the assembly of YHWH (*lo yavo Ammoni u-Moavi b-qhal YHWH gam dor asiri lo yavo lahem b-qhal YHWH ad olam*) is grounded in this etiology. Modern scholarly treatments (Sarna *JPS Genesis* 1989 pp. 139-140; Westermann *Genesis 12-36* 1985 pp. 313-314; Wenham *WBC Genesis 16-50* 1994; Hamilton *NICOT Genesis 18-50* 1995; Bauer *Reading Lot's Daughters* 1999) read the etymology as polemical-etiological rather than philological-historical: the Mesha Stele (ca. 840 BCE) preserves *Moab* without comment on the etymology, and the Akkadian and Egyptian textual references to *Moab* and *Ammon* are independent of the Hebrew etiology. The pair-etymology also produces the foundational tension of the book of Ruth: Ruth the Moabitess descends from the incest-line but enters the Davidic genealogy (Ruth 4:18-22), and the Ruth narrative is in part the canonical Hebrew Bible's working-through of the Deut 23:4-5 exclusion. Solomon's Moabite wives (1 Kgs 11), 2 Kgs 3 (the Moab campaign), and Neh 13:1-3 (the post-exilic re-application of the exclusion) extend the canonical reception of the etiology. The *moab-ammon-etiology-incest* entry documents the full cross-corpus context.
